opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think we're still quite early. If you look at the past year or so, the industry has clearly moved from "RL on math and code with verifiable answers" toward "RL on agents that actually do things": browsing, writing and running code in a sandbox, calling tools across many turns. That shift is real, and the gains are real. But if you ask how far we've gotten in *scaling* it, I'd say we've proven the direction works. We haven't yet found the clean scaling curve the way we did for pretraining.

A few things are holding us back. The first is the environment. In pretraining, data is basically text you can stream endlessly. In agent RL, every sample is a rollout in an environment, and building environments that are diverse, stable, and have reliable reward signals is extremely labor-intensive. Most teams are still hand-crafting them. Whoever figures out how to generate environments at scale, almost the way we generate synthetic data, will have a big advantage.

The second is infrastructure. Agent rollouts are long and uneven. One trajectory finishes in ten seconds, another waits on a tool call for minutes. So the classic synchronous RL loop wastes a huge amount of compute. A lot of the real engineering work right now is asynchronous rollout, partial rollouts, handling off-policy drift, keeping training stable when the data is stale. It's not glamorous, but it decides whether you can scale at all.

The third is reward and credit assignment over long horizons. When a task takes fifty steps and you only get a signal at the end, it's hard for the model to learn which decisions mattered. And once you go beyond verifiable tasks into open-ended work, the reward model itself becomes the bottleneck. Models are very good at finding loopholes in it.

So my honest view is that we're at roughly the stage pretraining was at a few years ago. People believe that more compute plus more environments yields better agents, and the early signs say yes. But the recipe isn't settled, and teams are still discovering basic things through trial and error. That's actually what makes it exciting. There's still a lot of room for small, focused teams to make real contributions.

r001.rationale: The response says agent RL is still early and lacks the clean scaling curve seen in pretraining, describing it as comparable to pretraining several years ago. This communicates a tentative assessment that its scaling results have not yet been as striking as pretraining’s.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think we're still in the very early innings. If you look at what happened over the past couple of years, the first big breakthrough was scaling RL on verifiable rewards, math and code, where you have a clean signal. That worked, and it worked much better than most people expected. But agent RL is a different beast, because now the model isn't producing one answer, it's taking a long sequence of actions in an environment, with tools, with partial observability, with delayed and often noisy rewards.

So where are teams actually at? I'd say the frontier labs have gotten agent RL to work reliably in a handful of domains: software engineering, browsing and search, some data analysis workflows. In those domains you can build an environment, you can define success reasonably well, and you can run thousands of rollouts. The gains there are real. But the moment you step outside those domains, the hard problems show up very quickly.

The first problem is environments. In pretraining, the data is the internet, it's just there. In agent RL, the environment is the data, and someone has to build it. A good environment needs to be realistic, it needs to be diverse, it needs to be hard enough that the model actually learns something, and it needs to have a reward signal that can't be gamed. Building that at scale is enormously expensive, and I think most people underestimate it. A lot of what looks like a modeling problem is actually an environment engineering problem.

The second problem is credit assignment over long horizons. When a trajectory is two hundred steps and the reward only comes at the end, figuring out which decisions mattered is genuinely difficult. People are trying process rewards, learned verifiers, decomposing tasks into subgoals, but none of it is a clean solution yet. And when the reward model is imperfect, the policy will find the holes. Reward hacking in agentic settings is much more creative than in single-turn settings, because the agent has more degrees of freedom.

The third thing, which I think gets less attention, is infrastructure. Agent rollouts are slow and heterogeneous. One trajectory takes thirty seconds, another takes twenty minutes because it's waiting on a sandbox or a tool call. Keeping thousands of GPUs busy when your data generation looks like that is a very different systems problem from pretraining. The teams that are ahead right now are often ahead because of their infrastructure, not because of some secret algorithm.

So if I had to put a number on it, I'd say we've maybe captured ten or fifteen percent of what's possible. The direction is clearly right, and the compounding is starting, you can see models getting meaningfully better at long tasks every few months. But the recipe is far from settled. I think the next two years are going to be defined by whoever figures out how to generate rich environments and reliable rewards at scale, more than by anything else.

r001.rationale: The response calls agent RL early-stage and its recipe unsettled, but never says its results have been less striking than scaling pretraining.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re still relatively early. The key question is what we mean by scaling agent reinforcement learning. Running more training jobs is one thing; reliably improving an agent’s ability to complete longer, more complex tasks is another.

With agents, you have to scale the environments, the interactions, and the quality of the feedback together. If a task takes many steps and fails at the end, how do you identify which decision caused the failure? And if the agent succeeds, how do you know it solved the task correctly rather than exploiting a weakness in the evaluation?

So I’d distinguish success in environments where outcomes are easy to verify from broad, dependable performance across unfamiliar tasks. The former gives us a useful path forward. The latter is where I think a lot of the difficult work remains. I wouldn’t claim to know exactly how far every team has gotten internally.

r001.rationale: The response says agent RL is still relatively early and that dependable performance remains difficult, but it does not compare its results with scaling pretraining or describe them as less striking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re still at an early stage. We’ve gotten better at scaling reinforcement learning for tasks where the outcome is easy to verify. But an agent has to take multiple actions, interact with an environment, and recover when something goes wrong. That makes the learning problem much harder.

The challenge isn’t simply to run more training. You need environments that are diverse enough, rewards that reflect whether the task was actually completed, and a way to learn from long trajectories. If an agent fails after twenty steps, which decision should you correct?

So I would distinguish between scaling the training system and scaling the capability. You can generate more trajectories, but the important question is whether that produces an agent that succeeds on unfamiliar tasks. I think that’s still an open question.

r001.rationale: The response says agent RL is still at an early stage and leaves capability scaling an open question, but it does not compare its results with scaling pretraining or say they are less striking.
